title: What Expository Preaching Actually Is
subtitle: A working definition of expository preaching set against topical and textual preaching, and why letting the text set the agenda forms a congregation over years.

sections.title: A Definition You Can Stand On
sections.body:
Expository preaching is not a style. It is a surrender.

The usual definitions are correct and useless. They say expository preaching explains the meaning of a passage in its context and applies it to the hearer. True. But the definition that will change how you study is shorter and harder. Expository preaching is preaching in which the point of the text is the point of the sermon, the shape of the text is the shape of the sermon, and the authority of the text is the only authority you bring into the room. You did not pick the message. You found it. Your job is to get out of its way.

This is the thing most preachers will not do. We come to the text with a message already in hand and go hunting for verses to dress it. We have something to say and the Bible becomes our witness, called to confirm what we decided in the car. That is not exposition. That is using Scripture. Exposition reverses the flow. The text speaks first, and you spend the week finding out what it said before you dare to say anything at all.

sections.title: Against Topical and Textual
sections.body:
Three kinds of preaching are not three flavors of the same thing. They put authority in three different places.

Topical preaching starts with a subject. Anxiety, marriage, money, forgiveness. You gather verses from across the Bible that touch the theme and arrange them into a case. Done with integrity it can be useful. Done badly, and it usually is, it becomes a man marshaling Scripture to support conclusions he already reached, the text reduced to evidence in a trial he is prosecuting.

Textual preaching takes a short passage, often a single verse, and uses it as a springboard. The verse opens the door and then the preacher walks off into the room of his own ideas. The verse is a launch pad, not a master.

Expository preaching refuses both moves. It takes a unit of text, a paragraph, a scene, an argument, and asks one question all week. What is this saying. Not what can I make it say. Not what would my people like to hear. What does it actually say, in its flow, in its context, on its own terms. Then it preaches that. The subject is whatever the text is about. The structure is whatever the text does. You are not the author. You are the usher.

sections.title: Letting the Text Set the Agenda
sections.body:
Here is the cost, and it is the whole point. When the text sets the agenda, you will preach things you would never have chosen.

You will land on a Sunday where the passage is about money and your largest givers are in the room. You will reach a verse on divorce the week a beloved family is falling apart. You will arrive at judgment when you wanted grace and at grace when you wanted to bring the hammer down. The lectio continua, preaching straight through a book, drags you to the texts you would have skipped. That is not a flaw in the method. That is the method working.

The preacher who chooses every topic preaches his own hobby horses for thirty years and never knows it. He has three or four messages and an infinite supply of verses. His congregation learns his obsessions. The expositor preaches the whole counsel of God because the book makes him, and over years his people get the full diet, the comfort and the warning, the doctrine and the lament, the parts that soothe and the parts that cut. I have stood in a pulpit and resented the next verse. That resentment was the Spirit telling me where I needed to preach.

sections.title: What It Forms Over Years
sections.body:
Exposition does not pay off on Sunday. It pays off in a decade.

A congregation fed week after week from the text learns something no single sermon can teach. They learn that the authority is in the book and not in the man. They watch you submit to the passage in front of them, and they learn to do the same in their kitchens. They learn how a paragraph works, how an argument moves, how a story turns, because they have watched you handle hundreds of them. You are not only feeding them. You are training them to feed themselves.

This is the quiet genius of it. The topical preacher creates dependence. His people need him to assemble the verses, because they cannot. The expositor creates competence. After ten years under faithful exposition, a member can open a chapter and find the point, because they have seen it done five hundred times. You are building Bereans, people who search the Scriptures to see whether these things are so.

That is the long obedience. It is unglamorous. It is slow. It will never trend. And it is the only kind of preaching that leaves behind a people who can stand when you are gone.

sections.title: How to Actually Begin
sections.body:
You do not need a seminar to start. You need a book and a discipline.

Pick a book of the Bible. Start small if you must, Jonah, Philippians, Ruth. Read it through in one sitting, more than once, before you carve it into preaching units. Then preach the units in order and do not skip. When the hard text comes, preach the hard text. When the boring genealogy comes, find why the Spirit put it there and preach that too.

Do the work of finding the author's point before you find your own. Ask what this passage meant to the people who first received it. Ask how it fits the argument around it. Ask where it points to Christ, because all of it does. Only then ask what it demands of the people in your room. The order matters. Meaning before application. Author before audience. Text before sermon.

This is harder than topical preaching and it will expose you faster. There is nowhere to hide in a verse you did not choose. But the man who preaches this way for thirty years will have handled the whole Bible, and his people will have heard the whole counsel of God, and that is the only legacy worth leaving from a pulpit. The book sets the agenda. You just keep showing up.
